the problem ↴

Math feedback tells students they're wrong — not why.

These are long-standing, well-documented challenges in math teaching and learning — not artifacts of any one product or platform.

  • ✕Feedback that doesn't diagnose. Across classrooms, worksheets, and digital tools alike, students mostly learn whether they were right — rarely what their reasoning got wrong. Formative-feedback research is clear that this is the part that moves learning.
  • ✕Cognitive load competes with reasoning. Math materials are often written above grade reading level, so learners spend their attention decoding the words instead of thinking about the math.
  • ✕Inconsistent standards. When feedback isn't reliable, students learn to guess at the rules and optimize for the grade rather than for understanding.
See how learning science shaped our response →
◆ Our design goalgrounded in formative-feedback research
Feedback should respond to a student's mathematical reasoning — helping them recognize a misconception and revise their thinking — rather than just marking an answer right or handing over the steps.
that's the bar!

the product ✏️

Four layers of scaffolding, chosen by diagnosis.

A rubric built from interviews with experienced tutors scores every submission on three dimensions — conceptual, procedural, explanation (0–2 each). The score decides which scaffold a learner sees next.

Triggered by: first incorrect answer

Low-intervention hints

The smallest nudge that redirects attention toward a productive path — a guiding question, never the answer. It's modeled on the first thing a human tutor would ask, and preserves the learner's chance to solve it themselves.

still stuck? → escalate to layer 2 ↓

real product ✓ the actual low-intervention hint, live in the whiteboard
Triggered by: second miss + conceptual error

Worked examples

When hinting isn't enough, the tutor models the full reasoning — one step at a time, with partially interactive visuals the learner completes along the way. Explicit modeling plus guided participation.

then prove it on a drill →

Fractions · Lesson 4 · Problem 1 of 5
real product ✓ the actual worked example, live in the whiteboard
Triggered by: after a worked example or procedural fix

Drill questions

Same knowledge component, friendlier numbers. The drill checks whether the learner can apply the support independently — not just follow along. Answer it right and you move on; miss it and you get concise corrective feedback, then continue.

back to independent solving ✔

Fractions · Lesson 4 · Problem 1 of 5
real product ✓ the actual drill question, live in the whiteboard
Triggered by: right answer, weak explanation

Sentence starters

A correct answer doesn't prove understanding. When the explanation scores 0–1, learners rebuild an ideal explanation via dropdowns — where the distractors are real misconceptions, so choosing correctly requires actual reasoning.

our process 🔍

Double diamond, evidence first.

Discover
Define
Develop
Deliver
Explore broadlyFocus the MVPBuild + testIterate + hand off

Discover Grounded in learning science

Literature across learning engineering, effective mathematics instruction, formative feedback, AI-supported learning, and prompt engineering — plus a scan of the current tool landscape. The underexplored opportunity: diagnosing the reasoning behind a wrong answer, not just the answer itself.

Discover Tutor interviews → the rubric

Semi-structured interviews with experienced tutors on how they evaluate work beyond correctness.

→Result: a 3-dimension rubric (conceptual · procedural · explanation, each 0–2) that powers the entire scaffolding brain.

Define User journey

We built a user journey to identify the common pain points learners may hit when working with an AI tutor — cognitive overload, platform trust, and a lack of learning-science-aligned interventions.

→Each pain point was mapped to a concrete MVP response in the feedback design.

Develop Prompt evaluation pipeline

We treated agreed human grades as ground truth and benchmarked LLM graders against them across providers and model sizes.

→Surprise: the smallest, cheapest model matched human judgment best (78–87% exact match) — bigger reasoning models over-corrected into harsher grading.

Develop Two rounds of usability testing

Round 1: 23 rising 5th–6th graders over Zoom. Round 2: in-person think-alouds. Diagrams became optional, the pen tool got fixed, and the recording button earned a real affordance.

Deliver What's next

We hand off our project to a mid-sized established ed-tech company. The handoff includes a working prototype of the whiteboard, a question bank, full documentation, and a roadmap for how to continue developing the product.
